clinicalPearls: The commonest inherited optic neuropathy, typically presenting in the first two decades with insidious, painless, bilateral and symmetrical loss of central vision
Colour vision is affected early, classically with a subtle blue-yellow (tritan) or generalised dyschromatopsia disproportionate to acuity
Fundus shows temporal or diffuse optic disc pallor, often with a characteristic temporal wedge of atrophy
Most cases arise from mutations in OPA1, a nuclear gene encoding a mitochondrial inner-membrane fusion protein, giving marked variability in severity even within one family
Visual fields typically show a centrocaecal or central scotoma reflecting preferential loss of the papillomacular bundle
A subset develop DOA-plus with sensorineural deafness, ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy or a mitochondrial myopathy
Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture supported by OCT thinning of the retinal nerve fibre layer and confirmed by genetic testing
Penetrance is incomplete, so mildly affected relatives may be unaware of any deficit
reference.pathophysiology: Dominant optic atrophy usually results from heterozygous mutations in OPA1, a nuclear-encoded protein embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane that governs mitochondrial fusion, cristae architecture and control of programmed cell death. Impaired mitochondrial dynamics render the metabolically demanding retinal ganglion cells vulnerable, with preferential degeneration of the small fibres of the papillomacular bundle. The result is progressive loss of ganglion cells and their axons, clinically expressed as central visual and colour deficits with temporal disc pallor. Because the mechanism is one of haploinsufficiency or a dominant-negative effect with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity, phenotype ranges from asymptomatic carriers to severe syndromic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Behr syndrome and other syndromic optic atrophies
Toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy (including B12 deficiency)
Compressive optic nerve or chiasmal lesion
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and macular ganglion cell complex
Formal colour vision assessment and automated perimetry
Pattern visual evoked potentials to document optic nerve dysfunction
Neuroimaging (MRI) to exclude a compressive or demyelinating cause
Targeted genetic testing for OPA1 and wider mitochondrial/optic atrophy gene panels
Audiometry and neurological assessment when a DOA-plus phenotype is suspected
redFlags: Rapid or markedly asymmetrical visual loss suggesting an alternative compressive or inflammatory cause
Additional neurological features (deafness, ataxia, neuropathy) indicating a DOA-plus syndrome
Pain on eye movement pointing towards optic neuritis rather than a hereditary atrophy
New field defect respecting the vertical midline suggesting chiasmal or retrochiasmal pathology
reference.prognosis: Vision usually declines slowly and often stabilises at a moderate level, with most patients retaining useful sight, though a minority progress to legal blindness and DOA-plus cases carry additional systemic morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing early symptoms to refractive error or amblyopia and missing the hereditary pattern
Overlooking mildly affected relatives because of incomplete penetrance
Assuming a diagnosis without imaging and thereby missing a compressive lesion
Failing to screen for the systemic features of DOA-plus
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: No proven disease-modifying therapy; management focuses on low-vision rehabilitation with visual aids, magnifiers and support for education and work
Avoidance of mitochondrial toxins such as tobacco and excess alcohol, with caution over drugs that impair mitochondrial function
Regular ophthalmic monitoring with acuity, colour vision, visual fields and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Audiometry and neurological review for DOA-plus features such as sensorineural deafness, ophthalmoplegia and peripheral neuropathy
Registration as sight-impaired where appropriate with provision of low-vision services
Multidisciplinary input including ophthalmology, clinical genetics and audiology
Genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal dominant OPA1 inheritance with variable expressivity
